articles.author: ryanlee
articles.description:
Signup tests often fail in a way that is hard to reproduce. The form works on a laptop, but the CI job sometimes reads an old verification message, waits for a code that belongs to another run, or leaves a test inbox behind. The usual response is to increase the timeout. That makes the symptom quieter, not the test more reliable.
The better fix is a small contract between the test, the application, and the email fixture. Every run gets an identity, every message is matched to that identity, and cleanup has an owner even when the assertion fails. This pattern is useful whether the inbox comes from a fake emails generator, a local mail catcher, or a service that can create temporary mail.
Consider a Playwright test that submits a signup form and then searches an inbox for the latest message.…
articles.title: React Signup Tests Need a Run-Scoped Email Contract

articles.description:
Short answer: put each user reminder on a queue, make the consumer idempotent, retry transient delivery failures with backoff, and move exhausted work to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) for deliberate redrive. For a rate-limited e-commerce worker pool, the best queue is the one whose recovery controls your team can operate at 02:00, not the one with the longest feature list.
This choice starts with an evaluation constraint: a checkout follow-up may be delivered once, but it must never be intentionally sent twice just because a worker lost its lease. Email and webhook providers can time out or return HTTP 429. Queue delivery is at-least-once, so the awkward case is a worker that sends successfully and crashes before acknowledging the message. Retries are expected. Duplicate side effects aren't.
T…
articles.title: Rate-Limited Reminder Recovery: Idempotent Queues After Webhook and Email Send Failures

Most AI sessions begin with a blank slate. You open Claude Code, pick up where you left off in a data pipeline, and spend the first few minutes re-explaining the schema decisions you made two days ago, the library you chose over an alternative, the edge case that came up in a review. Starting from zero is not a limitation of the models; it is a gap in the tools that sit around them.

articles.author: Landstrider
articles.description:
Most guides on Telegram Stars monetization get one thing wrong, and it quietly wrecks your revenue planning: they treat the ~30% app-store fee as if it were deducted from the developer's Stars payout. It is not. It inflates the buyer's price. The developer's per-Star rate is fixed and flat.
I built a free calculator to make this concrete, but here is the arithmetic first, taken from Telegram's own payments table.
For purchases made inside the App Store or Google Play, Telegram assigns a fixed monetary value per Star to the developer:
50 Stars → buyer pays $0.99 → developer gets $0.65
500 Stars → $9.99 → $6.50
1000 Stars → $19.99 = $6.00 (Apple/Google 30%) + $0.99 (Telegram admin) + $13.00 (developer)
2500 Stars → $49.99 → $32.50
Read the 1000-Star row carefully. The buyer's $19.99 splits t…
articles.title: Telegram Stars payouts: the app-store cut hits the buyer, not you

articles.description:
An avatar pipeline fails operationally when it treats a generated URL as identity. TL;DR: in an Express service, upload the original once, resize from the returned asset ID into a fixed set of three render sizes, store every derivative ID with the user, and resolve delivery URLs only when rendering. This preserves image quality where it is visible without making every client download the largest file, and it keeps a future URL or delivery-policy change out of the user table.
For a gaming profile, I would use three semantic slots such as avatar, roster, and thumbnail, not a matrix built from every screen and pixel density. The exact dimensions are a product decision; the invariant is the fixed set. A request succeeds only after the database record points to the complete new set. Until then,…

articles.description:
Everyone blames the host. "I need to upgrade my plan." Nine times out of ten, the host is fine — the site is just carrying dead weight. Here's how I find it.
Don't guess. Run your URL through PageSpeed Insights and write down three numbers: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint), INP (Interaction to Next Paint), and TTFB (Time to First Byte). These are your before numbers. Everything below is about moving them.
If TTFB is over 600ms on a cached page, then you can blame the host. Under that, keep reading.
1. No page caching. This is the big one. Every uncached WordPress request boots PHP, hits MySQL, renders the theme — hundreds of milliseconds you don't need to spend. A caching plugin serving static HTML cuts that to near zero. This alone fixes most "slow WordPress" complaints.
2. Unoptimized imag…
articles.title: Why Your WordPress Site Is Slow (It's Probably Not Your Host)

articles.description:
In May 2025 Shopify's admin replaced the printed Financial Summary with an on-screen Finances summary.
So I built a page that reproduces it from the Admin GraphQL API. Matching Shopify's figures turned out to be mostly a question of definitions and dates, not arithmetic.
Every amount comes back as shopMoney.amount, a string. scalars/Decimal describes it as "A signed decimal number, which supports arbitrary precision and is serialized as a string."
I never add those strings as floats. I parse each one into integer minor units, sum integers, and only format at the end. The precision comes from Intl: 2 for USD, 0 for JPY, 3 for KWD.
The second rule is about signs. Every reduction is stored as a negative number: discounts, returns, shipping discounts, reversed tax, refunded payments. Then ever…
articles.title: Rebuilding Shopify's Finances summary from the Admin GraphQL API, line by line
